clinicalPearls: Presents as rapid growth of fine, soft, non-pigmented lanugo hair, often beginning on the face (including the nose and eyelids) and spreading caudally to the trunk and limbs, sparing only the palms and soles.
A strong marker of underlying, often advanced malignancy; lung, colorectal and breast carcinoma are the commonest associations.
In women breast and gynaecological tumours predominate, while in men lung and colorectal cancers are most frequent.
The eruption of malignant down may appear before the tumour is diagnosed and typically indicates advanced or metastatic disease.
It is frequently accompanied by glossitis with painful tongue papillae and by other paraneoplastic signs such as acanthosis nigricans and tripe palms.
It must be distinguished from drug-induced hypertrichosis and from androgen-dependent hirsutism, which follows a female terminal-hair pattern.
Florid facial lanugo growth produces a characteristic elongated, simian facies, often with accompanying weight loss and cachexia.
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism of acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa is incompletely understood. Tumour-derived factors are thought to reset hair follicles from the resting or vellus state into active production of lanugo-type hair, possibly through altered growth-factor signalling and disturbance of the normal androgen-independent follicular cycle. The resulting hair is fine and unpigmented, resembling foetal lanugo, which distinguishes it from the pigmented terminal hair of androgen-driven hirsutism. The frequent association with advanced malignancy and cachexia suggests a humoral, tumour-related aetiology.
additionalDifferentials: Hirsutism from androgen excess (polycystic ovary syndrome, adrenal or ovarian tumour)
Hypertrichosis of anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition
Porphyria cutanea tarda with localised facial hypertrichosis
additionalInvestigations: CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify an occult primary
Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening (mammography, colonoscopy, gynaecological assessment)
Skin and scalp examination with dermoscopy confirming fine lanugo hair
Tumour markers guided by the suspected primary
Review of the drug history to exclude iatrogenic causes
redFlags: Rapid development of fine lanugo hair on the face of an adult
Accompanying weight loss, cachexia or glossitis
Coexisting acanthosis nigricans or tripe palms
reference.prognosis: Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa usually signifies advanced or metastatic malignancy and therefore carries a poor prognosis; hair growth may regress following successful tumour treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing lanugo hypertrichosis with androgen-driven hirsutism
Overlooking a drug cause before attributing the eruption to malignancy
Failing to appreciate that it often indicates advanced disease
Not examining for accompanying paraneoplastic signs and glossitis
